## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Littajātaka* (Ja 91) is a narrative belonging to the Pali *Jātaka* collection. According to the frame narrative recorded in the commentary, the Buddha told this story while residing at Jetavana to address the unreflective or thoughtless use of monastic requisites (*apaccavekkhitaparibhoga*) by the monks [Fausböll 1877]. The canonical verse opens with *Littam paramena tejasā ti* [Fausböll 1877]. In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta was a wise gambler (*paṇḍitadhutto*) who coated a gambling die with poison to catch and expose a cheating partner who habitually swallowed the die whenever he was about to lose [Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1877]. In the *samodhāna* (connection), the Buddha draws a moral comparison, warning that the thoughtless use of requisites is just like the reckless ingestion of deadly poison (*apaccavekkhitaparibhogo nāma apaccavekkhitvā katavisaparibhogosadiso hoti*) [Sahni 2008; Fausböll 1877]. Modern scholars cite the tale in discussions of Buddhist ethics as an illustration of the tension between intention (*cetanā*) and apparent rule-breaking, where the Bodhisatta's poisoning of the die functions to reform the cheat [Appleton 2010], as well as in the context of early Buddhist virtues and environmental ethics concerning consumption [Sahni 2008].

 DharmaNexus detects four internal Pali text-reuse matches with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (matching up to 348 characters between §0.4–1.4 and §2325_8–2328), reflecting the transmission of the verses within the traditional commentary, and identifies no cross-language matches [DharmaNexus].
